p: (in the piyut for the blessing Atah Gibbor):
"And may He remember for you the merit of the one who declared,
And it is found in Midrash Rabbah
would I not have been dust?
would I not have been ash?" etc.
with mesiras nefesh beyond the strict law,
that is, giving up his life
in this world and in the World to Come.
For in the test of the fiery furnace of Nimrod
לֹא הָיָה מְצוּוֶּה עַל קְדוּשַּׁת הַשֵּׁם
he was not commanded regarding Kiddush Hashem,
שֶׁבֶּן נֹחַ אֵינוֹ מְצוּוֶּה עַל זֶה
for a Ben Noach is not commanded about this,
"But your blood of your lives I will demand," etc.,
And according to the Rambam's view
(פֶּרֶק ה מֵהִלְכוֹת יְסוֹדֵי הַתּוֹרָה הֲלָכָה ד)
one of whom it is said,
"Let him transgress and not be killed,"
who was killed rather than transgress —
he is liable for his own life;
only because there burned within him
did he give over his life, and his soul as well;
and even if he would lose, chas v'shalom,
his share in the World to Come,
that the Name of Heaven be sanctified through him
and His Divinity, blessed be His Name, become known.
So too in the war of the four kings,
zeal for Hashem burned within him
for there had been no war in the world, etc.;
and a murderer is liable to death
and even according to the view
שֶׁהָיוּ שְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת וּשְׁמוֹנָה עָשָׂר אִישׁ כִּפְשׁוּטוֹ
that there were literally three hundred eighteen men,
against the armies of the four kings?
for it was only from the zeal for Hashem
to do the will of Hashem Yisbarach,
even though he was not obligated
בְּפִנְחָס בְּקַנְאוֹ אֶת קִנְאָתִי [בְּמִדְבַּר כה, יא]
with Pinchas, "when he avenged My zeal" (Bamidbar 25:11):
yet one who comes to ask is not instructed so,
for he is not obligated to endanger himself,
he would not be executed for him;
רַק מִי שֶׁבּוֹעֵר בְּלִבּוֹ קִנְאַת ה׳
only one in whose heart the zeal for Hashem burns
is in the category of zealots
וְלָכֵן אָמַר לוֹ מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ לְפִנְחָס
Therefore Moshe Rabbeinu said to Pinchas,
"Let the one who reads the letter
be the one to carry it out"
(כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ כָּל זֶה בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין פב, א)
(as they said all this in Sanhedrin 82a),
for since the zeal burns within him,
he is in the category of zealots, etc.
וְכֵן הָיָה עִנְיַן אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
And so was the case of Avraham Avinu, a"h,
in the war of the kings;
and this is what they said in the Midrash,
And this is what he said:
would I not have been dust,
would I not have been ash?" —
רַק שֶׁה׳ יִתְבָּרַךְ הִסְכִּים עַל יָדוֹ
only Hashem Yisbarach concurred with him
and performed a miracle for him,
because he intended the will of Hashem Yisbarach
Then, since he became lowly in his own eyes,
to be like dust and ashes,
he had already merited the level of Atika,
כִּי כֹה אָמַר רָם וְנִשָּׂא וְגוֹ׳
"For thus says the High and Exalted One," etc.,
"On high and in holiness I dwell,
and with the crushed and lowly of spirit," etc.
"High and Exalted," "on high and in holiness,"
and it is written, "and with the crushed,"
So too with Avraham Avinu, a"h:
and then he said, "I am dust and ashes"
(this is what they said in Chullin 89a,
then he merited what is written,
and he merited the level of Atika,
which is "High and Exalted, on high and in holiness."
But to be refined in all the middos,
for it is written after the Akeidah (Bereishis 24:1),
"And Avraham was old, coming into days" —
that he was refined in the three upper levels,
יוֹמִין עִלָּאִין [זֹהַר חֵלֶק א קכט, א].
For then he gave himself over
he would not have had to heed
that His Divinity, blessed be His Name, become known
and Hashem Yisbarach Himself had told him,
כִּי בְיִצְחָק יִקָּרֵא לְךָ זָרַע [בְּרֵאשִׁית כא, יב]
"For through Yitzchak shall offspring be called yours" (Bereishis 21:12);
so that His Divinity, blessed be His Name, become known,
even forfeiting his own World to Come,
as he did in the test of the furnace
and the war of the four kings,
according to the middah of his love
the middah of fear to an extreme degree,
and feared to transgress His will, Yisbarach,
lest he had some personal bias in the matter
out of love for his son;
and then he became integrated into Fire,
And this is what is said at the test of the Akeidah,
"What does it matter if I do not understand?
Then he was refined in all the middos,
and this is what is said, "coming into days" —
שֶׁהוּא כְּנֶגֶד אַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת עוֹלָמוֹת דְּכִיסּוּפִין
corresponding to the four hundred worlds of longing,
in each of the four worlds,
as stated above (in the previous ma'amar).
And this is why we then say,
"Remember for me the shekels of Efron," etc.
"Greater is what is said of Moshe
than what is said of Avraham, etc.;
of Moshe and Aharon it is written,
became a chariot for the middah of Ayin, Nothingness,
as they said in the holy Zohar
"And wisdom — from where shall it be found":
from the place called Kodesh HaKodashim" —
that is, the middah of Ayin,
which is Atika, the most concealed
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (שָׁם סד, ב).
as they said in the holy Zohar (there, 64b).
וְכֵיוָן שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
And since Moshe Rabbeinu, a"h, became
a chariot for the middah of Ayin,
he merited to be the root
of all the words of Torah,
וְעַל כֵּן זָכָה מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
all the crowns of Matan Torah
from the six hundred thousand souls of Yisrael
וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּמִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא (כִּי תִשָּׂא ג)
And this is what they said in Midrash Tanchuma (Ki Sisa 3):
"By your life, just as you stand now
that they read it before Me,
it is as if you stand there
and raise up their heads, etc.;
'Lift up the head' is not said,
The point is that in truth
the essential lifting of the head
עַל יְדֵי מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
who is the root of the words of Torah;
by making a calf before Me;
be careful with 'we will hear,'" etc.
נֶגֶד קְדוּשַּׁת יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
corresponds to the holiness of Yaakov Avinu, a"h,
דְּאִיתָא (תִּקּוּנֵי זֹהַר תִּקּוּן יג כט, א)
as it is found (Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 13, 29a):
Rather, he was from the inner side;
this one from the body, and that one from the soul" —
from whom comes the root of the holiness
of all the bodies of Yisrael,
and this is the crown of "we will do."
who is the root of all the words of Torah,
which are the root of the six hundred thousand
souls of the generation of the wilderness;
and he corresponds to the crown of "we will hear."
And the essential lifting of the head
עַל יְדֵי כֶּתֶר נִשְׁמָע שֶׁלֹּא בִּטְּלוּ
is through the crown of "we will hear," which they did not annul;
which is to rectify the sin of the Calf,
the essential lifting of the head
that, chas v'shalom, after his passing
the lifting of the head would cease
that every year, with the reading of the parsha,
it is as if Moshe stands
there is a power from Moshe Rabbeinu,
namely, the power of the Torah that each one has.
And this is what they said in the Gemara
וְאַף שֶׁזֶּה אָמַר מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
And although Moshe Rabbeinu, a"h, said this
"What does Hashem your God ask of you
כִּי אִם לְיִרְאָה וְגוֹ׳ [דְּבָרִים י, יב]
that is, with respect to the power of the Torah,
in the manner of what they said (Chullin 93a),
which Rashi explains as a talmid chacham;
that is, in every talmid chacham
the portion of Torah within him
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר [דְּבָרִים לג, ד] תּוֹרָה וְגוֹ׳
"It is not written here 'the congregation of Yannai,'
And this is what they said:
that every year when Parshas Shekalim is read
it is as if Moshe stands
through the power of the Torah,
as they said, "Be careful with 'we will hear.'"

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 49:11 — “Avraham answered: 'Had Amrafel killed me, would I not have been dust? Had Nimrod burned me, would I not have been ashes?' The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: 'By your life! You said, I am dust and ashes; by your life, I shall give your children atonement through them,' as it says, 'They shall take for the impure person some of the dust of the burning of the sin offering,' and 'A pure man shall gather the ashes of the cow.'” The Midrash connects Avraham's humility to rescue both from battle and from the furnace, and makes his words a continuing source of merit for his descendants. Rav Tzadok explains the exceptional self-surrender underlying those two rescues.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 74b–75a; Rambam, Hilchos Melachim 10:2 — “They asked Rabbi Ami: Is a descendant of Noach commanded regarding sanctification of the Name, or is he not? Abaye said: Come and hear: The descendants of Noach were commanded seven commandments; if this were so, there would be eight. Rava answered: The seven include their associated requirements. What was the conclusion? Rav Adda bar Ahavah said: They say in Rav's school that Naaman asked forgiveness for bowing in the house of Rimmon while his master leaned on his arm, and Elisha told him: 'Go in peace.'” The ensuing objection distinguishes private from public conduct. Rambam states the conclusion explicitly: 'A descendant of Noach whom a coercer forces to violate one of his commandments is permitted to violate it. Even if forced to serve idols, he may do so, because they are not commanded regarding sanctification of the Name.' Rav Tzadok takes this as the legal background against which to describe Avraham's extraordinary act of love.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 34:13; Rashi on Genesis 9:5 — “'But'—this includes one who strangles himself. Could it apply even to one like Shaul? Scripture says 'but,' limiting the rule. Could it apply to those like Chananyah, Mishael and Azaryah? Scripture says 'but,' limiting the rule.” Rashi explains 'your blood' as blood shed by a person who kills himself, and 'for your lives' as including even one who strangles himself without shedding blood. The Midrash also states exceptions; Rav Tzadok's discussion concerns how Avraham's pre-Sinai act stands in relation to the ordinary rule. This passage is 34:13 in the checked digital edition, rather than the manuscript's 34:8.

paragraphs.text: Rambam, Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah 5:4 — “Anyone of whom it is said, ‘Transgress rather than be killed,’ who is killed rather than transgresses, is accountable for his own life. Anyone of whom it is said, ‘Be killed rather than transgress,’ who is killed and does not transgress, has sanctified the Name. If this was before ten Israelites, he has sanctified the Name publicly, like Daniel, Chananyah, Mishael, Azaryah, Rabbi Akiva and his companions. These are the martyrs above whose degree there is none.” Rambam distinguishes the two legal duties. Rav Tzadok quotes this formulation as background to Avraham's willingness to risk even his spiritual standing; the exceptional interpretation of Avraham's motive is Rav Tzadok's own argument.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Lech Lecha 7 — “Another interpretation: 'The wicked have drawn the sword'—these are the four kings, Amrafel and his companions. There had not yet been war in the world; these came and opened with the sword and made war. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to them: 'You opened with the sword to cast down the poor and needy; their sword shall enter their own hearts.' Avraham arose and killed them.” The Midrash identifies the four kings as the initiators of the violence and applies the reversal in Psalms 37:14–15 to their defeat. Rav Tzadok develops this as the object of Avraham's zeal.

paragraphs.text: Nedarim 32a — “'Three hundred and eighteen': Rabbi Ami bar Abba said: Eliezer was equal to them all. Some say: It was Eliezer alone, for the numerical value of his name is that number.” The two readings are distinct: in the first Eliezer equals the entire force, while in the second the number 318 itself signifies Eliezer. Rav Tzadok argues that even the literal force was small beside the four kings' armies.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 42:8 — “'The fugitive came': Reish Lakish said in Bar Kappara's name: This was Og, the fugitive. Why was he called Og? He came and found Avram occupied with the commandment of cakes. He did not intend for the sake of Heaven, but said: 'This Avraham is a fiery zealot. I shall now tell him that his brother's son has been taken captive; he will go to war and be killed, and I shall take his wife Sarai.'” The characterization occurs in Og's calculating speech, not as the Midrash's unqualified legal ruling. Rav Tzadok draws from it Avraham's readiness to act from burning zeal despite the danger.

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Vayishlach 6 — “Although he judged them as murderers—and a murderer is liable to death under the laws of the descendants of Noach—according to Torah he was not required or permitted to endanger himself by going alone with Eliezer. ... It was only because of his great ardor and zeal; he knew that, since the wish to pursue the kings had arisen in his will, the will of Hashem was to rescue Lot. In truth this was Hashem's will because of the soul of David and Mashiach that would issue from his descendants. ... Since Hashem performed a miracle for him, he evidently acted fittingly and attained the Divine intention beyond human comprehension.” The earlier passage explicitly separates the ordinary legal assessment from Rav Tzadok's explanation of Avraham's exceptional intuition. It also identifies rescue of the future Davidic line as the providential purpose of rescuing Lot.

The following Gemara quotation sets out the exceptional legal conditions of the act to which Rav Tzadok compares Avraham's action.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 82a — “Rav Chisda said: If a person comes to seek a ruling, he is not instructed to act. ... Moreover, had Zimri withdrawn and Pinchas killed him, Pinchas would have been liable for killing him. Had Zimri turned and killed Pinchas, he would not have been liable, for Pinchas was pursuing him. ... What did Pinchas see? Rav said: He saw the deed and recalled the law. He said to Moshe: 'My father's father's brother, did you not teach me when you came down from Mount Sinai that zealots may strike one who has relations with an Aramean woman?' He answered: 'Let the reader of the letter himself be its messenger.'” The source describes the act as narrowly conditioned and not a course authorized through ordinary consultation. Rav Tzadok compares Avraham's self-endangering zeal to this exceptional category; he does not derive a general duty to take such risks.

paragraphs.text: Isaiah 57:15 — “For thus says the high and exalted One, who dwells forever and whose name is holy: I dwell on high and in holiness, and with the crushed and lowly of spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly and to revive the heart of the crushed.” The verse joins Divine exaltedness with dwelling beside the lowly. Rav Tzadok sees in this conjunction the access to the hidden, highest degree attained through Avraham's self-abasement.

paragraphs.text: Sotah 5a — “'And with the crushed and lowly of spirit': Rav Huna and Rav Chisda differed. One said: 'The crushed one is with Me'; the other said: 'I am with the crushed one.' It is more reasonable to follow the one who says 'I am with the crushed one,' for the Holy One, blessed be He, left all the mountains and hills and rested His Shechinah upon Mount Sinai; Mount Sinai did not rise upward.” The preferred reading describes the Shechinah descending to the humble, rather than the humble being physically raised. It supplies the specific meaning of 'I am with the crushed one' used here.

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Toldos 1 — “At the trial of the binding it is written, 'Now I know that you fear God': this is Yitzchak's quality, while Avraham's quality was love, as it says, 'Avraham who loves Me.' ... From his extraordinary fear he was afraid to violate Hashem's word, suspecting himself lest some personal attachment to his son be influencing him. ... This is 'Avraham was crowned through Yitzchak': Avraham's completeness up to the supernal crown came through Yitzchak's quality. ... Avraham was crowned through fear, and Yitzchak through love; as the Zohar says, water was included in fire and fire in water.” The selected clauses of the cited maamar directly explain why completion of Avraham's love requires the contrary quality of fear. Its intervening discussion also describes the reciprocal completion of Yitzchak through Avraham.

paragraphs.text: Genesis 21:12; 22:12 — “God said to Avraham: 'Do not let the matter of the boy and your maidservant be grievous in your eyes. Whatever Sarah tells you, listen to her voice, for through Yitzchak your offspring will be called.' ... He said: 'Do not stretch out your hand against the lad, and do nothing to him; for now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only one, from Me.'” The first verse states the promise concerning Yitzchak; the second, spoken at the end of the binding, identifies Avraham's fear of God. Rav Tzadok explains the trial as obedience beyond Avraham's own understanding of how the promise and the command would be fulfilled.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, Kedushat Levi, Vayera, paragraph 35 — “There are two kinds of performance: a person may carry out a commandment while knowing its reason, or carry it out without knowing its reason. Doing it without knowing its reason is greater, for when the reason is known, it is not evident that he acts from love of the Creator: perhaps he acts because he knows the reason. When he acts without knowing the reason, it is evident that everything is done from love of Hashem.... After the angel announced, ‘Do not stretch out your hand against the lad,’ it became clear retroactively that Avraham’s desire to offer his son upon the altar came from love of Hashem, rather than from a reason. For if there were a reason requiring Yitzchak to be offered, why did the angel command that he not be offered?... Since there was no such reason, everyone knew Avraham’s intention: he had done all this solely from fear of Hashem.”

paragraphs.text: Chullin 89a — “Rava said, or some say Rabbi Yochanan: What is said of Moshe and Aharon is greater than what is said of Avraham. Concerning Avraham it is written, 'I am dust and ashes'; concerning Moshe and Aharon it is written, 'What are we?' Rava said, or some say Rabbi Yochanan: The world endures only on account of Moshe and Aharon. Here it is written, 'What are we?' and there it is written, 'He suspends the earth upon nothing.'” This is a distinct statement from the earlier list of humble responses. Rav Tzadok makes the contrast between 'dust and ashes' and 'what are we?' the basis of Moshe's association with ayin, nothingness.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II, Mishpatim 121a — “It is written, 'Wisdom—from where is it found?' Torah issues from wisdom, from the place called Holy; wisdom issues from the place called the Holy of Holies. Rabbi Yitzchak said: The Jubilee too is called Holy, for it is written, 'It is a Jubilee; it shall be holy for you.' Israel includes these degrees, as it is written, 'You shall be men of holiness to Me.'” The word me-ayin in Job 28:12 can be heard as 'from ayin,' the hidden source beyond wisdom. Rav Tzadok uses the Zohar's hierarchy of Torah, wisdom and the Holy of Holies to explain Moshe's rootedness above ordinary apprehension.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II, Beshalach 64b — “Rabbi Abba said: What is meant by ‘Is the Lord in our midst, or nothing?’ Were Israel fools who did not know this matter? Had they not seen the Divine Presence before them and the clouds of glory surrounding them? ... Rather, Rabbi Shimon said this: They wished to know the difference between the Ancient One, concealed beyond all concealment, who is called Nothing, and Zeir Anpin, who is called the Lord. ... Why, then, were they punished? Because they made a separation and put it to a test. They said: If it is this One, we will ask in one manner; if it is this One, we will ask in another manner. Therefore, immediately, ‘Amalek came.’” The Zohar interprets Israel's question at Massah as a question about the degree from which Divine governance was being revealed. It explicitly names the concealed Atika as Ayin.

paragraphs.text: Shemos Rabbah 27:9 — “A king told his servants: 'Guard these two delicate cups for me; take care with them.' As a servant entered the palace, a calf lying at the entrance gored him and one cup broke. The servant stood trembling before the king. 'Why are you trembling?' the king asked. 'A calf gored me and broke one of the two cups.' The king answered: 'If so, take care with the second.' So the Holy One, blessed be He, said: 'At Sinai you poured Me two cups, We shall do and We shall hear. You broke We shall do, making a calf before Me; take care with We shall hear.' Thus, 'Hear the word of Hashem, house of Yaakov.'” This parable preserves 'We shall hear' as the surviving channel of fidelity after the Calf. Rav Tzadok relates it to Moshe, the inward root of Torah, and to the renewed elevation through reading the shekalim passage.

paragraphs.text: Chullin 93a; Rashi, s.v. Moshe — “Rabbi Abba said in Rav Yehudah's name, in Shmuel's name: The blood vessels in the foreleg are forbidden. Rav Safra said: 'Moshe! Did the Merciful One say, Do not eat meat?' Rava said: 'Moshe! Did the Merciful One say, Eat blood? Cut it and salt it, and it is permitted even for cooking in a pot.' Rashi explains: 'Moshe—a Torah scholar.'” Moshe functions here as an honorific address to a scholar in a halachic debate. Rashi's gloss supplies the specific usage from which Rav Tzadok develops his account of each scholar's Torah share as a part of Moshe.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra Rabbah 9:3 — “The guest arose and seized Rabbi Yannai, saying: 'My inheritance is with you, and you are withholding it from me!' He asked: 'What inheritance of yours is with me?' He answered: 'Once I passed a school and heard the children's voices saying, Moshe commanded us the Torah, an inheritance of the congregation of Yaakov. It does not say the congregation of Yannai, but the congregation of Yaakov.' He asked him: 'How did you merit to eat at my table?' He answered: 'In all my days I have never repeated an evil report to the person spoken about, and I have never seen two people fighting without making peace between them.' Rabbi Yannai said: 'You possess all this proper conduct, and I called you a dog!' He applied to him: 'One who orders his way'—one who appraises his conduct is of great worth.” Rabbi Yannai had found that his guest lacked learning and had disparaged him. The guest's protest establishes that Torah is the inheritance of every member of Yaakov's congregation, including the unlearned; his conduct then reveals the worth Rabbi Yannai had overlooked.

paragraphs.text: Pesikta Rabbasi 10, the passage cited as section 11 — “The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moshe: 'Moshe, exalt this nation as much as you can, for it is as though you exalt Me.' It says, 'When you lift up the head of the children of Israel.' It does not say, 'When you lift up the children of Israel,' but 'the head'; Israel's head is none other than the Holy One, blessed be He, as it says, 'Their king passed before them, and Hashem at their head.' To what is this comparable? To someone fashioning a crown and setting precious stones and pearls in it. A passerby saw him and said: 'Set into it as much as you can, for it is destined to be placed upon the king's head.' ... So the Holy One said to Moshe: 'Take care with this nation: of all the nations I created, it was the first to proclaim Me King, as it says, This is my God, and I will glorify Him.'” The crown parable makes Israel's elevation an adornment of the Divine King. The digital edition presents this within chapter 10 without the manuscript's section number; the exact passage and proof verse were checked.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra Rabbah 24:9 — “Likewise: 'You shall be holy.' Could this mean like Me? Scripture therefore says, 'For I am holy': My holiness is above your holiness.” The Midrash's plain comparison preserves the distinction between Divine and human holiness. Rav Tzadok next cites a chassidic rereading of the same words: the holiness manifested above is 'from your holiness.' His ensuing argument relates the two readings.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra Rabbah 24:4 — “The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moshe: 'Go, say to Israel: My children, just as I am separate, so shall you be separate; just as I am holy, so shall you be holy.' Thus it is written: 'You shall be holy.'” This passage commands imitation, while the preceding passage maintains that Divine holiness exceeds human holiness. Rav Tzadok explains how separation from worldly absorption can lead to a continually deeper recognition of that transcendence.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 39a — “The Sages taught: 'Sanctify yourselves and you shall be holy.' If a person sanctifies himself a little, he is sanctified greatly; if he sanctifies himself below, he is sanctified above; if he sanctifies himself in this world, he is sanctified in the World to Come.” The response from above exceeds the person's initial act below. Rav Tzadok explains this increasing sanctification as the capacity to perceive a holiness still beyond what one has attained.

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Yisro 7 — “Hashem is beyond all apprehension, and the description 'holy' does not apply to Him in Himself. It is only because Israel recognizes His holiness—this recognition being that He is holy, separated from every apprehension—that Hashem is called holy. ... 'You are holy, enthroned upon the praises of Israel': through Israel's praises He is called holy, because they recognize His holiness and kingship.” The English selects the precise clauses relevant to the present argument. Rav Tzadok's earlier discussion grounds the designation 'holy' in Israel's recognition and praise; it does not suggest a change in God's essence.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Kedushas Levi, Vaera, s.v. Vaera el Avraham — “In truth, the more a person sanctifies and purifies himself and serves Hashem, the more he knows that he has not yet begun to serve Him at all. A person who thinks he already serves Hashem shows that he is not serving Him; were he serving Him, he would know how far he is from Hashem. This is 'My holiness recedes ever higher above your holiness': the more you add to your sanctification, the more you see that you are far from the Holy One's holiness. ... Alternatively, it may be explained through the Sages' statement that Israel adds strength to the heavenly company. The more Israel sanctifies itself, the more it adds strength and holiness above. This is 'My holiness above is from your holiness': through your holiness My holiness is elevated and exalted ever higher.”

Kedushas Levi, Vaera, s.v. Vaera el Avraham

— “In truth, the more a person sanctifies and purifies himself and serves Hashem, the more he knows that he has not yet begun to serve Him at all. A person who thinks he already serves Hashem shows that he is not serving Him; were he serving Him, he would know how far he is from Hashem. This is 'My holiness recedes ever higher above your holiness': the more you add to your sanctification, the more you see that you are far from the Holy One's holiness. ... Alternatively, it may be explained through the Sages' statement that Israel adds strength to the heavenly company. The more Israel sanctifies itself, the more it adds strength and holiness above. This is 'My holiness above is from your holiness': through your holiness My holiness is elevated and exalted ever higher.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Kedushas Levi states both readings invoked here: growth in holiness reveals greater distance from God, and Israel's sanctification increases the manifestation of holiness above. Rav Tzadok connects them by locating the latter in the deeper recognition that human sanctification makes possible.

paragraphs.text: Genesis 41:32 — “As for the dream being repeated to Pharaoh twice: the matter is firmly established by God, and God is hastening to do it.” Yosef explains why Pharaoh saw the same decree in two dreams. Rav Tzadok applies the conjunction of confirmation and haste to the doubled sanctity of Shabbos and the shekalim reading.
